strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in vision-based robotic manipulation: independently moving targets. DOMINO is a potentially valuable contribution, with 117,000 demonstrations, 35 tasks, five embodiments, and three motion-complexity levels. Its value extends beyond the proposed algorithm.

The paired static/dynamic task design provides useful evidence of current policies' sensitivity to target motion. The scalable demonstration-generation pipeline and extensive per-task results could support further research on this problem.

PUMA achieves a meaningful improvement on the main benchmark: 17.20% success versus 10.86% for the Qwen3-VL-based OpenVLA-OFT baseline. Using a shared backbone strengthens this comparison. The appendix adds a history-aware ContextVLA baseline, history-length and prediction-horizon ablations, data-scaling experiments, and higher-complexity evaluations.

The physical-robot experiments provide encouraging supporting evidence: PUMA achieves 42% average success versus 24% for π0.5 across five tasks. Reporting end-to-end inference latency and explicitly acknowledging stop-on-contact dynamics, deployment delays, and sim-to-real limitations improves the paper's transparency.
weaknesses: The central interpretation that PUMA learns object-motion anticipation is insufficiently established. Masked average pooling of DINO features does not explicitly preserve object position or velocity, so future-feature prediction could primarily regularize object identity, appearance, or manipulation state. Tables 8 and 12 show that the auxiliary objective helps, but there are no matched current-feature, temporally shuffled-feature, or scene-level prediction controls, nor direct measurements of predicted motion. The oracle experiment likewise does not isolate missing history as the cause of control instability. These gaps matter because the claimed mechanism is a principal distinction from existing predictive-query approaches.

The benchmark only partially captures the dynamic manipulation capabilities emphasized in the paper. Objects follow prescribed kinematic trajectories, and autonomous motion ends upon gripper contact (§B.2, §D.3). Demonstrations replay static plans synchronized to target arrival. This is useful for interception but offers limited evidence for sustained tracking under contact or response to interaction-induced disturbances. Additionally, the limitations section indicates that realistic inference delays are not incorporated into benchmark evaluation; standalone latency measurements do not establish performance when targets continue moving during computation.

The generalization claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Most results cover one embodiment, clean scenes, and Level 1 motion; the other embodiments and randomized appearances are not substantively evaluated. Higher-level results involve target-level training or adaptation rather than zero-shot transfer, and Table 13 gives only modest absolute gains when training directly on those levels. Dynamic-to-static transfer is also mixed: Tables 17 and 19 show ACT falling from approximately 27.7% to 14.0% and π0.5 from 44.8% to 22.5%, although OpenVLA-OFT improves. Selected positive examples do not establish broadly improved spatiotemporal representations.

Important benchmark reproducibility details remain unspecified. Despite useful optimizer and architecture settings, the manuscript does not clearly document training demonstrations per task and experimental condition, held-out scene/trajectory construction, seed separation, or the simulator control timestep and action-chunk execution schedule. No repeated-training variability or confidence intervals are reported. The project and code fields are blank in the supplied manuscript, leaving the substantial dataset contribution difficult to independently inspect.

Some transfer comparisons do not adequately separate architecture benefits from training history. Table 5 emphasizes PUMA adapted from Level 1 against π0.5 trained directly on the target level; the appendix partially addresses this with direct-training results, but lacks a similarly adapted π0.5 control. In the physical experiments, PUMA explicitly starts from its simulation checkpoint, while equivalent initialization and adaptation details for competing methods are unclear. A PUMA comparison with and without simulation pretraining is needed to substantiate the claimed sim-to-real transfer benefit.

Several benchmark definitions need reconciliation. The main text defines α as a maximum speed, but Level 2 generation constrains average speed (§D.3). Table 14 reports α in [0.5, 1.5] while labeling the evaluation DOMINO@0.1, leaving unclear whether these are absolute speeds or multipliers. The manipulation score is based on terminal end-effector distance and the better-performing arm, which does not directly measure sustained tracking or bimanual completion; its claimed bounded range also requires clipping absent from the stated formula. These ambiguities affect interpretation of difficulty and execution quality.

strengths: DOMINO addresses an important gap in vision-based robot learning: manipulation of independently moving targets. Its 117,000 demonstrations, 35 tasks, five embodiments, and three motion-complexity levels constitute a potentially useful benchmark contribution, independently of PUMA’s algorithmic novelty.

The synchronized demonstration-generation pipeline is a practical contribution. Paired static and dynamic tasks help expose a substantial performance gap: for example, π0.5 falls from 44.8% static success to 7.5% zero-shot dynamic success.

PUMA provides a credible empirical improvement on the principal evaluation: 17.20% success versus 10.86% for the Qwen3-VL-based OpenVLA-OFT baseline. The shared-backbone comparison and ablations support the usefulness of combining historical optical flow with auxiliary future-feature supervision.

The supplementary material meaningfully strengthens the evidence through a history-aware baseline, history-length and prediction-horizon ablations, higher-complexity experiments, data scaling, and detailed per-task results. Physical experiments also provide encouraging evidence, with 42% average success versus 24% for π0.5 across five tasks.

The paper appropriately attributes its underlying frameworks and pretrained components, reports implementation and latency details, and explicitly acknowledges stop-on-contact dynamics and missing inference-delay modeling.
weaknesses: The benchmark’s construction limits what its results establish about dynamic manipulation. Demonstrations replay static plans while object trajectories are back-calculated to meet those plans, and autonomous motion stops upon gripper contact. This provides scalable interception data but does not demonstrate sustained tracking under externally driven post-contact motion or expert recovery from unexpected disturbances. The resulting trajectory–action correlations warrant a control using independently sampled motion and a reactive expert. These acknowledged simplifications are consequential to the breadth of the claims.

The proposed mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Mask-averaged DINO features may emphasize object identity and appearance rather than spatial motion; the paper does not measure how much future position or velocity they encode. Table 8 lacks an auxiliary-prediction-only condition and a current-frame feature-supervision control, so the gains do not establish that forecasting dynamics, rather than generic representation regularization, is responsible. Similarly, the oracle experiment’s small improvement does not demonstrate that missing history causes its control instability.

The generalization conclusions overstate the evidence. Tables 17 and 19 show that dynamic-only training reduces average static success from 27.74% to 13.97% for ACT, 17.51% to 14.09% for OpenVLA-OFT, and 44.83% to 22.54% for π0.5. Selected positive examples therefore do not support the broad claim in Finding 3. Higher-level results involve target-level adaptation, and the real-world experiment lacks a PUMA control without simulation pretraining to isolate the claimed transfer benefit. Most evaluations also cover only one embodiment and clean scenes.

Important benchmark details remain ambiguous despite the substantial appendix. Training counts per configuration, train/test separation, and the timing relationship between observations, action-chunk execution, and object motion are not sufficiently specified. Motion definitions also conflict: Level 1 sampling is uniform in the main text but clipped half-normal in the appendix, while α bounds maximum speed in the main text but average speed for Level 2 in the implementation description. Table 14 needs clarification of whether [0.5, 1.5] denotes absolute speeds or multipliers, since α otherwise has units of m/s.

The Manipulation Score needs stronger justification. Final end-effector proximity does not reliably measure completion of multistage manipulation, and selecting the better arm can conceal bimanual failure. The stated progress formula does not inherently remain within [0, 100] and can have a zero denominator; clipping and numerical handling are unspecified. No validation establishes that this metric tracks manipulation quality beyond success rate.

Experimental uncertainty and comparison controls are incomplete. Results lack training-seed variability or confidence intervals, which matters particularly for small higher-level gains and 20-trial physical evaluations. The cross-level comparison gives PUMA additional Level 1 pretraining without an equivalent baseline condition. Overall, the useful benchmark and promising performance gains make the decision close, but unresolved protocol validity and causal attribution concerns favor borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in embodied computer vision: manipulating independently moving targets. I assess it as Algorithms/General, while giving substantial credit to DOMINO as a benchmark contribution. The combination of a useful evaluation platform and a demonstrably stronger policy supports a borderline acceptance.

DOMINO offers substantial scale and structure: 117,000 trajectories, 35 tasks, five embodiments, and three motion-complexity levels. The synchronized demonstration-generation pipeline is a practical contribution, and paired static tasks help expose the difficulty introduced by target motion.

PUMA achieves a meaningful improvement under the main evaluation protocol: 17.20% success versus 10.86% for the Qwen3-VL OpenVLA-OFT implementation, with manipulation score increasing from 30.49 to 34.97. Using the same backbone strengthens this comparison. Low absolute success is not itself disqualifying for a challenging new benchmark.

The experimental coverage is substantial. It includes numerous baselines, per-task results, history-length and prediction-horizon ablations, a history-aware baseline, higher-complexity experiments, data scaling, and static/dynamic co-training. These results support the practical value of combining optical flow with auxiliary future-feature supervision.

Physical-robot experiments provide encouraging additional evidence: PUMA achieves 42% average success across five tasks versus 24% for π0.5. The appendix supplies useful implementation details, and the discussion candidly acknowledges contact simplifications, deployment latency, and the sim-to-real gap.
weaknesses: The evidence supports a narrower notion of generalization than the title and several conclusions suggest. Most experiments use one embodiment, clean backgrounds, and constant-velocity motion. Higher-level results cover ten tasks and involve target-level training or adaptation; cross-embodiment, unseen-task, and domain-randomization generalization are not established. The real-world setup closely matches simulation and uses task-specific demonstrations.

The benchmark simplifies a central aspect of dynamic interaction: targets follow prescribed kinematic motion until gripper contact, after which autonomous motion is released. This limits its coverage of sustained tracking and post-contact dynamics. Moreover, Appendix F explicitly leaves inference-aware evaluation to future work. Reporting inference speed separately does not establish that simulation rankings reflect policies acting while targets continue moving during computation.

The proposed mechanism is not fully isolated. Masked average-pooled DINO features do not explicitly supervise position or velocity, so their prediction could improve object representation without learning motion anticipation. There is no auxiliary-only ablation, current-frame or temporally shuffled supervision control, or matched scene-level prediction comparison. The oracle experiment also does not establish that missing history causes control instability when ground-truth future trajectories are already supplied.

The broad claim that dynamic training fosters better static-task representations is overstated. Tables 17 and 19 show average static success dropping from 27.74% to 13.97% for ACT, 17.51% to 14.09% for OpenVLA-OFT, and 44.83% to 22.54% for π0.5 when replacing static training with dynamic training. Selected task-level improvements demonstrate transfer, but not a general static-performance benefit. Co-training gains also need a matched total-data and training-budget control.

Statistical and training-protocol reporting limits confidence in smaller improvements. Simulation uses 100 episodes per task, but repeated training seeds and uncertainty estimates are absent; physical experiments use only 20 trials per task. It is also unclear whether real-world baselines receive comparable simulation pretraining to PUMA. Exact training-subset sizes, held-out split construction, and baseline tuning budgets should be specified more clearly.

Several benchmark definitions need reconciliation for reproducibility. Section 2 defines α as maximum speed, whereas Appendix D constrains average speed for Level 2. Appendix E calls α=0.05 out of distribution despite the Level 1 training sampler including speeds down to 0.01, and the randomized α range [0.5, 1.5] needs clarification as an absolute speed bound or multiplier. The route-completion formula also requires clipping and zero-denominator handling to guarantee its stated range; proximity of either arm alone is an incomplete measure of multi-stage task progress.
